text: RACI is a standard model used across many fields to map every major decision to specific people, and it exists to kill ambiguity, not add bureaucracy. Applied to an incident response team, it answers a question that sounds simple but causes real damage when left unanswered: during a live incident, who actually gets to decide?

Responsible is whoever does the work. Accountable is whoever owns the decision and answers for the outcome -- and there should be exactly one Accountable person per item, never several. Consulted means giving input before the decision gets made. Informed means being told afterward, with no input expected at all.

A real IR team maps onto four core roles. The Incident Commander holds overall decision authority and coordinates the team. The technical lead runs the hands-on investigation, containment, and eradication. The communications lead manages internal updates and, when needed, external statements, so nobody technical is improvising a public statement mid-incident. The legal and compliance liaison advises on notification duty, privilege, and evidence handling.

Take the decision to pull a production system offline for containment. The technical lead is Responsible -- they execute the isolation. The Incident Commander is Accountable -- they weigh the business impact and give the go-ahead. Legal is Consulted first, since taking a system offline can affect evidence or a contractual uptime obligation. The CEO is Informed afterward, told what happened rather than asked to approve it live.

Collapsing Responsible and Accountable into one blurry idea is where things go wrong. Without a clear matrix, the technical lead might isolate the system on their own authority while, at the exact same moment, the CEO is telling someone else to keep it running -- a direct conflict playing out in real time, during the one moment an organization can least afford it.

That's exactly what a RACI matrix prevents: one name per major decision, agreed and written down before any incident, not negotiated during one. Next, Lesson 8 puts this plan, these playbooks, and these exact roles through a tabletop exercise -- testing all of it before a real incident tests it for you.
